intro: SaaS Quick Ratio compares the MRR you're adding against the MRR you're losing, as a single growth-versus-churn number. Enter new, expansion, churned, and contraction MRR to get the ratio.

sections.heading: How SaaS Quick Ratio is calculated
sections.body: SaaS Quick Ratio = (New MRR + Expansion MRR) ÷ (Churned MRR + Contraction MRR) — [the same growth-over-loss shape Wall Street Prep uses to define the metric](https://www.wallstreetprep.com/knowledge/saas-quick-ratio/). Existing customers who neither churned, contracted, nor expanded never enter the calculation at all — the ratio only looks at MRR that moved during the period, not the stable base sitting still underneath it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: ($15,000 + $5,000) ÷ ($4,000 + $1,000) = $20,000 ÷ $5,000 = 4.00x. For every dollar of MRR lost to churn and contraction this period, $4 was added from new and expansion — a read on growth relative to loss, not a statement about total revenue or profitability.

sections.heading: What one ratio number can hide
sections.body: [Wall Street Prep's own treatment of this metric is explicit that a strong Quick Ratio measures growth efficiency relative to churn specifically](https://www.wallstreetprep.com/knowledge/saas-quick-ratio/) — it doesn't say anything about whether the business is profitable or sustainable beyond that one relationship, which is exactly the gap [Rule of 40](/calculators/rule-of-40) is built to check instead by pairing growth against profit margin rather than churn. A 4.00x ratio built mostly on new-logo MRR reads very differently from the same 4.00x built mostly on expansion MRR from existing accounts, since new-logo growth usually carries a much higher acquisition cost behind it that this ratio never sees. The same source notes that "not all revenue is created equal" — the ratio treats every dollar of New, Expansion, Churned, and Contraction MRR as interchangeable, when the story behind each of those four numbers can be very different.

sections.heading: SaaS Quick Ratio vs. NRR
sections.body: Both use the same four MRR movement types, but combine them differently. SaaS Quick Ratio divides gains (new + expansion) by losses (churned + contraction) — a ratio with no reference to where MRR started. [NRR](/calculators/nrr) instead measures the existing customer base specifically: starting MRR plus expansion, minus contraction and churn, divided by that same starting MRR — new-logo MRR is deliberately excluded. A company can post a strong Quick Ratio driven mostly by aggressive new-customer acquisition while its NRR, which only tracks how existing customers behaved, stays flat or declines. The two aren't reading the same thing, even though they're built from overlapping inputs.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Treating a high Quick Ratio as proof of overall business health. It measures growth relative to churn specifically — it says nothing about profitability, cash burn, or acquisition cost behind the growth.
Not distinguishing whether the ratio is being driven by new-logo MRR or expansion MRR. The two usually carry very different acquisition costs, even though the formula weighs them identically.

Reading a ratio below 1.0 as always alarming without checking the absolute dollar amounts. A small MRR base can swing the ratio sharply from one or two account changes in a way a larger base wouldn't.

Comparing Quick Ratios across companies measured over different period lengths (monthly vs quarterly) without adjusting. A longer window captures more churn and more expansion, which moves both sides of the ratio.

faq.q: What is the SaaS Quick Ratio?
faq.a: The SaaS Quick Ratio is a leverage metric that compares MRR gained against MRR lost in a period, calculated as (New MRR + Expansion MRR) divided by (Churned MRR + Contraction MRR). A ratio of 4.00x means $4 of MRR was added for every $1 lost to churn and contraction during that period. Unlike NRR, which tracks only the existing customer base, Quick Ratio includes new-logo MRR in its numerator, so it captures growth from both new customers and existing-account expansion together, measured against everything lost from churn and downgrades in the same window. Customers who neither expanded, contracted, churned, nor were newly acquired don't appear in the calculation at all.

faq.q: How do you calculate the SaaS Quick Ratio?
faq.a: Add new MRR and expansion MRR for the numerator, add churned MRR and contraction MRR for the denominator, then divide: Quick Ratio = (New + Expansion) ÷ (Churned + Contraction). A company with $15,000 in new MRR, $5,000 in expansion MRR, $4,000 in churned MRR, and $1,000 in contraction MRR has a ratio of ($15,000 + $5,000) ÷ ($4,000 + $1,000) = 4.00x. All four figures need to come from the same period — mixing a monthly new-MRR figure with a quarterly churn figure produces a ratio that doesn't describe any real period accurately. If churned and contraction MRR both happen to be zero, the ratio is undefined rather than infinite.

faq.q: What is a good SaaS Quick Ratio?
faq.a: A ratio of 4.00x is widely cited as a reference point in SaaS finance writing, meaning $4 of MRR added for every $1 lost — but that number describes growth efficiency relative to churn specifically, not overall business health, profitability, or sustainability. A company can hit 4.00x while burning significant cash to acquire the new-logo MRR driving it, or while its existing customer base is quietly shrinking and the ratio is propped up entirely by new sales. The ratio is most meaningful read alongside where the growth is actually coming from (new vs. expansion) rather than compared against a flat target on its own.

faq.q: How is SaaS Quick Ratio different from NRR?
faq.a: Quick Ratio divides all MRR gained (new plus expansion) by all MRR lost (churned plus contraction), with no reference point tied to where MRR started. NRR measures only the existing customer base: starting MRR plus expansion, minus contraction and churn, divided by that same starting MRR — new customers are deliberately left out entirely. A company can post a strong Quick Ratio driven mostly by new-logo sales while its NRR, which only reflects how existing customers behaved, stays flat or even declines. They're built from overlapping inputs but answer genuinely different questions about where growth is actually coming from, and a strong reading on one doesn't guarantee a strong reading on the other.

faq.q: What does a SaaS Quick Ratio below 1.0 mean?
faq.a: A ratio below 1.0 means more MRR was lost to churn and contraction than was gained from new and expansion MRR in that period — the recurring revenue base shrank overall, even if some individual accounts grew. That's a real, valid result worth investigating, not a calculation error. It's worth checking the absolute dollar amounts before reacting strongly, though: on a small MRR base, one or two large account changes can swing the ratio sharply in either direction in a way that wouldn't move the needle much on a larger base experiencing the exact same dollar-value changes in either direction.

Metric-specific section (what-a-single-ratio-hides) directly sourced from Wall Street Prep's own stated limitation ('not all revenue is created equal') plus an independently-derived point about new-logo vs expansion MRR carrying different acquisition costs the ratio can't distinguish. Edge case (denominator = 0 -> undefined, catalog's own documented edgeCase, 'show - not Infinity') and the below-1.0 case (a real, valid shrinking-MRR result) both covered, the latter with an independently-computed small-base sensitivity note.
